openers.how-soils-form: Every soil has a history, written by place, environment and time. This chapter follows that history, the development called soil formation. Five intertwined influences steer it: parent material, climate, topography, organisms and time. Vasily Dokuchaev in 1898 and Hans Jenny in 1941 each tried to capture them in a single equation. Along the way come water carrying dissolved material down through the profile, chains of different soils strung down a single slope, and ancient soils that formed in the past under conditions long gone.

soil-form-042.title: How bare rock slowly becomes living soil
soil-form-042.text: In the Mediterranean climate of Sicily, weathering makes new soil at roughly 1/10 mm a year. That slow work is soil formation, also called pedogenesis: the development of soil as shaped by place, environment and history. It begins with the {{ref:soil-found-052}} of freshly accumulated parent material. New soils then deepen through further weathering and through deposition, including settling dust. Microbes feed on the nutrients that weathering releases. They produce organic acids and proteins that speed the breakdown of minerals, and their residues help build the dark, decayed organic matter of the topsoil. As the soil develops, pioneer species arrive first, then richer plant and animal communities through ecological succession. Topsoil deepens as remains of dead plants and microbes accumulate and mix with weathered minerals. With maturity come layers. Accumulating organic matter, mineral weathering and the washing of dissolved material downward create horizons that differ in color, structure, texture and chemistry. Biogeochemical processes both build and destroy order within a soil. Differences in the conditions that shape soils produce patterns in where soil types occur. Pedogenesis is studied as a branch of pedology. It explains how soils are spread across the land today and how they were spread in past geological periods.

soil-form-050.title: Leaching: how water strips a soil from the top down
soil-form-050.text: Water soaking down through a soil does not travel empty. Leaching is the removal of soluble materials from one zone of a soil to another by water moving through the profile. It differs from eluviation, which moves tiny mineral and organic particles, called colloids, rather than dissolved material. Both tend to strip the topsoil and enrich the subsoil, in a horizon called the zone of illuviation. Climate sets the pace directly. Leaching is most intense in warm, humid regions where the soil does not freeze. The red tropical soil described in {{ref:soil-form-065}} develops under high temperatures and heavy rainfall, and intensive leaching leaves it less fertile than other soils. Its signature shows in the profile. In one brownish leached soil, {{ref:soil-class-049}}, water washes mobile chemicals out of the A horizon. Iron and aluminum oxides, the subject of {{ref:soil-form-085}}, gather in the B horizon and color it rusty orange-brown. The Canadian system for naming soils marks strongly leached layers as light gray Ae horizons. In Solonetzic soils, progressive leaching moves salts and sodium downward. The process can also defeat reclamation: intensive leaching has left reclaimed acid sulfate soils infertile.

soil-form-043.title: Five forces behind every soil, from climate to time
soil-form-043.text: Every soil on Earth answers to the same five intertwined influences: parent material, climate, topography, organisms and time. These are the soil-forming factors. Reordered as climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, they spell the acronym CLORPT. Parent material, the mineral material a soil forms from, becomes soil as it is weathered, transported, deposited and precipitated. Climate is regarded as the dominant factor, and soils show the distinctive marks of the climate zones in which they form. Topography can either hasten or slow the work of climate. Each soil also has its own mix of microbial, plant, animal and human influences. Time acts through all the others. How long a profile takes to develop depends strongly on climate, parent material, relief and living things. The factors once sorted the soils of a whole nation. An early US scheme, {{ref:soil-class-012}}, divided soils into three orders according to their dominant factors. In one of them, a local factor of relief or parent material outweighed the zonal effects of climate and vegetation.

soil-form-072.title: Paleosols, soils from vanished worlds
soil-form-072.text: Some soils formed more than 2.5 billion years ago. A paleosol is an ancient soil that formed in the past. Geologists use the word for a former soil buried under sediments such as alluvium or loess, or under lava or volcanic ash. In older deposits it has hardened into rock. Soil scientists mean a soil formed long ago whose properties bear no relation to today's climate or vegetation, found on old cratons and outliers of ancient rock. Over the last 50 million years, drying climates hardened former tropical soils across much of Australia into crusts so unweatherable that only poorly developed soils form on them. These relict soils are exceedingly infertile, yet often hold exceptional biodiversity. Paleosols also keep records. Pollen, carbon isotopes and leaf waxes in them reveal past plant life, including the balance of C3 and C4 plants. Glacial loess layers separated by paleosols record glaciations, and stacked paleosols help reveal past earthquakes.

soil-form-044.title: Climate, the dominant hand in shaping soil
soil-form-044.text: Where warmth and plentiful water meet in a soil, weathering, leaching and plant growth all run at their peak. Climate works chiefly through temperature and effective precipitation: rainfall minus the water lost to evaporation and plant transpiration. Together they set the rates of chemical, physical and biological processes. Water must first penetrate the regolith, and the deeper it goes, the deeper the soil weathers and develops. Percolating water carries clay and dissolved organic material from upper layers to lower ones, separating horizons. In dry regions, salts are not leached. They can build up enough to curb plant and microbial growth, while carbonates accumulate in hard layers. Colder or drier climates fix less carbon as organic matter but also decompose less of it. So profiles are more distinct in wet, cool climates than in wet, warm ones, where organic matter is quickly consumed. Climate also acts through vegetation: trees in humid climates, grasses in subhumid and semiarid regions, shrubs in arid lands.

soil-form-046.title: Snails, fungi and fire: life as a soil builder
soil-form-046.text: In the Negev desert, land snails grazing on lichens process between 0.7 and 1.1 metric tons of limestone per hectare each year, starting soil formation. Organisms, meaning plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and humans, form one of the soil-forming factors. Microorganisms drive key mineral transformations. Some bacteria fix nitrogen from the air, and some fungi extract deep phosphorus and add carbon to the soil. Plants hold soil against erosion and build organic matter. Working with fungi and bacteria around their roots, they release chemicals that break down minerals. Burrowing animals mix soil and open pores for water and gases. That mixing tends to undo the processes that create distinct horizons. Old burrows in lower horizons often fill with A-horizon material, leaving features called crotovinas or krotovinas. Humans belong here too, and with them fire. Clearing, tillage, irrigation, fertilizer and lime can change soil formation abruptly. Neolithic fires set by people are now accepted as helping form the soils of {{ref:soil-class-123}} and {{ref:soil-class-053}}.

soil-form-047.title: Time: from fresh flood mud to a developed profile
soil-form-047.text: A fresh layer of flood mud shows no soil development at all. The old surface lies buried beneath it, and soil formation starts anew in the deposit. Time is the span over which the other soil-forming factors interact, and it shapes how far a soil has developed. Texture and clumping alone do not make a developing soil; a distinct B horizon does. A profile takes from decades to several thousand years to form, depending strongly on climate, parent material, relief and living things. Even stable landscapes, some lasting millions of years, keep gaining, losing and altering material. The soil life cycle ultimately ends in conditions that leave the soil vulnerable to erosion, though most cycles are long. Researchers study time by comparing soils of different ages that differ little otherwise, and through paleosols, which record earlier conditions. The very idea of development toward a mature profile has critics. They argue that soil never stops changing, because the soil-forming factors themselves keep fluctuating.

soil-form-045.title: Slope, height and aspect: how relief shapes soil
soil-form-045.text: On a steep slope, soil is lost quickly to erosion, and less rain soaks in. Soils there tend to be shallower and less developed than those on nearby level sites. Topography, or relief, shapes soil through slope, elevation and aspect, the direction a slope faces. It controls runoff, erosion and the formation of the surface profile. Soils at the foot of a hill get more water, and slopes facing the sun's path are drier than those that do not. Gravity carries water, dissolved substances and fine particles downslope, enriching the ground at the foot of hills and mountains. In swales and hollows where runoff collects, the regolith weathers more deeply and profiles are more advanced. In the lowest spots, saturation restricts drainage and aeration. Weathering and decay slow, while iron and manganese are lost faster, and wetland soils, saline marshes or peat bogs may form. Recurring patterns of relief produce repeating sequences of soils, explored in {{ref:soil-form-054}}.

soil-form-048.title: Dokuchaev writes soil as an equation
soil-form-048.text: {{ref:soil-hist-001}}, often called the father of pedology, reached his conclusion in 1883: soil forms over time under climate, vegetation, topography and parent material. In 1898 he wrote it as an equation, soil = f(cl, o, p) tr. Soil is a function of climate, organisms and parent material, and tr is relative time: young, mature or old. Jenny's later version, {{ref:soil-form-049}}, differs in two ways. It treats time as a full factor, and it adds topographic relief.

soil-form-049.title: Jenny's equation and its open-ended list of factors
soil-form-049.text: In 1941 the pedologist in {{ref:soil-hist-010}} wrote soil formation as S = f(cl, o, r, p, t, ...). Soil is a function of climate, organisms, relief, parent material, time, and whatever else may matter. The trailing dots were deliberate. Unlike Dokuchaev's equation, Jenny's treats time as a factor, adds relief, and leaves room for more state variables as understanding improves. It is often remembered by the mnemonic Clorpt. The equation can be solved by deduction or empirically. The empirical route, varying one factor while holding the others constant, is the one mostly used today. It produced a family of models: climofunctions, biofunctions, topofunctions, lithofunctions and chronofunctions. Since 1941, soil surveyors worldwide have used the equation as a qualitative checklist of the factors behind a region's soil pattern. Critics grant that the five-factor model is parsimonious and useful. They argue it leaves out biodynamic processes, such as those that produce buried layers of stones.

soil-form-051.title: Modeling how irrigation water flushes out salt
soil-form-051.text: All irrigation water contains salts, so irrigated land must be flushed. A leaching model is a hydrological model of how irrigation water washes dissolved substances, notably salt, out of soil. It describes the process over time and against the amount of water applied, depending on the water regime and the soil's properties. Leaching is used to reclaim salty soil or keep irrigated land's salt content favorable. Curves from the Chacupe pilot area in Peru show deeper-layer salt first rising as salts arrive from the topsoil, then falling as more water percolates. Models such as {{ref:soil-water-237}} help set drainage requirements.

soil-form-054.title: The catena: a chain of soils down one hillside
soil-form-054.text: On a hillside at Bukalasa in central Uganda, the chemist W.S. Martin described soils changing in sequence from top to bottom. Geoffrey Milne named the pattern catena, Latin for chain. A catena is a series of distinct but co-evolving soils arrayed down a slope, all in the same climate and on the same parent material. The slope divides into ridge, crest, midslope and toeslope. Crests drain freely. Steep middle facets erode faster and are thinner and drier. The flatter top and bottom carry thicker, deeper soils, and toeslopes are wetter, poorly drained and richer in clay and organic matter. Upper facets lose materials such as salts by eluviation, and lower facets gain them by illuviation. A catena is an open system. Its sequence becomes predictable when climate is uniform along the slope and each facet's inputs and outputs reach equilibrium. A mature catena balances erosion and deposition. In wet western Scotland, on acid schists, one catena runs from peat bog to peaty forms of the bleached soil described in {{ref:soil-class-138}}.

soil-form-080.title: Pedoturbation: the churning that blurs soil layers
soil-form-080.text: Soil horizons are not sealed compartments. Clays churn, frost heaves and animals burrow, and material crosses from one layer to the next. Pedoturbation is this mixing of material between horizons, an important factor in soil formation. It includes the churning of clays, cryoturbation, and mixing by living things. It transforms soils through destratification, mixing and sorting. It also opens preferential paths for air and infiltrating water. Mixing by animals tends to counteract the processes that create distinct horizons. Together with weathering and the build-up of decayed organic matter, animal mixing is a main process in forming one order of deeply weathered tropical soils. Not every disturbance counts. When surface salts precipitate, they disrupt soils locally, but they do not mix horizons, so they are not pedoturbation. Pedoturbation belongs to a wider family called perturbation: the pedological and sedimentary processes that change water-borne alluvial sediments and soils in place over time.

soil-form-055.title: The biomantle, the living upper skin of soil
soil-form-055.text: In the stable humid tropics, termites, ants and worms work year-round, and the churned upper soil often reaches 5–6 m or more. In the midlatitudes it is often less than 1–2 m thick. This is the soil biomantle: the organic-rich, animal-mixed upper part of a soil, including the topsoil, where most soil organisms live, reproduce and die. It is mainly a product of organic activity. Animals, plants and fungi mix and destratify the parent material, and often sort its particles. In a midlatitude A-E-B-C profile, the biomantle is everything above the B horizon. As originally defined, it must show at least 50% biofabric, the pelleted fabric made by invertebrates. Light and full of channels, it speeds water downward and, above dense subsoils, sideways downslope. Two-layered biomantles have a basal layer of stones and form in mixed fine and gravelly material. One-layered ones form in uniform sands, loess or gravels. In some desert, mountain and freshly eroded bedrock soils, the biomantle is the whole soil.

soil-form-063.title: Chronosequences: centuries read from months of fieldwork
soil-form-063.text: Forest development takes decades or centuries, yet a chronosequence lets researchers study it from field data gathered in a few months. A chronosequence is a set of sites that share similar attributes but differ in age. In soil science, the sites have developed for different lengths of time, with only small differences in the other soil-forming factors, so they reveal time as a factor. A classic use traces plant and microbial succession on recently deglaciated ground. One 2005 study used distance from a glacier's nose as a stand-in for site age. Along a chronosequence, a cambic horizon develops into a clay-enriched Bt horizon as the soil matures. The method has a weak point. It assumes that nothing but age differs between sites, and this often cannot be tested. Its use in field studies of succession has therefore been debated.

soil-form-085.title: Sesquioxides: the iron and aluminum oxides that color soils
soil-form-085.text: A sesquioxide is an oxide with two atoms of an element for every three of oxygen, such as Fe2O3 and Al2O3. Many contain a metal in the +3 oxidation state. In soil, the ones that matter are the oxides of iron and aluminum. Their movements show up as color. One strong form of leaching, {{ref:soil-form-061}}, washes them out of the A horizon down to the B horizon, where they build a red-orange layer. In another process, {{ref:soil-form-081}}, silica is leached away while sesquioxides stay behind, giving many tropical soils their red color. Horizon notation marks their build-up with suffixes: s for illuvial and o for residual accumulation.

soil-form-065.title: Laterite, the brick-red earth of the tropics
soil-form-065.text: In 1807 Francis Buchanan-Hamilton named a formation in southern India laterite, from the Latin later, brick. The compact soil cuts easily into building blocks. Laterite is a kind of soil rich in iron and aluminum that often forms in hot, wet areas, mostly in the tropics. Nearly all laterites are rusty red from their high iron oxide content. Yves Tardy calculated that they cover about one-third of Earth's continental land, including most land between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. On one plateau in Madhya Pradesh, India, the laterite cap is 30 m thick. Laterites outside today's humid tropics formed when the land lay near the equator. They are read as signs of climatic change, continental drift or both. The term itself is disputed. It has been applied to cemented sesquioxide-rich horizons, any reddish surface soil, a rock type, whole weathering profiles and even a theory of weathering. Researchers such as Paton, Williams and Ollier call the usage confused, and some urge abandoning the word.

soil-form-061.title: Podzolisation: acid litter bleaches the upper soil
soil-form-061.text: Under boreal pines, a light, ash-pale layer can form just beneath the dark surface. Podzolisation is the extreme form of leaching behind it: it eluviates iron and aluminum sesquioxides from the upper soil. It generally occurs where precipitation exceeds the water returned to the air by evaporation and plants. The chemistry starts in the litter. Decaying organic matter releases organic acids that act as chelating agents, molecules that grip metal ions. Under conifers, a thin litter layer yields an acidic decaying layer called mor, at pH 4.5, rich in these agents. They break down clay and release iron and aluminum, which become sesquioxides and move from the A horizon down to the B horizon. Bases such as calcium and potassium wash out too. Quartz and silica remain, in a light, eluviated AE horizon at the base of the A horizon. Below, the B horizon holds a dark layer of illuviated organic matter and bases over a red-orange layer of sesquioxides. If water saturates the A horizon above the B horizon, mottling or gleying follows. The process is especially intense in boreal and cool temperate pine forests, whose litter is rich in phenolic compounds and the organic acid described in {{ref:soil-chem-060}}. Tropical forests show little or none.

soil-form-066.title: Laterization: rain, drought and millions of years
soil-form-066.text: Laterization was most active from the mid-Tertiary to the mid-Quaternary, 35 to 1.5 million years ago, and it has not stopped. It is the prolonged chemical weathering of rock under tropical conditions that produces laterite. It needs high temperatures and heavy rainfall alternating with dry seasons. Rain leaches the rock, and in the dry season capillary action lifts the dissolved ions to the surface. Acid dissolves the host minerals. Hydrolysis precipitates insoluble iron and aluminum oxides, while sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium are leached away. Solutions of the right pH dissolve silica in preference to the iron and aluminum oxides, leaving mainly those two metals behind. The first products are weathered rocks called saprolites, and quartz is the most abundant mineral surviving from the parent rock. Gentle crests and plateaus help by protecting the weathered cover from erosion. The parent rock shapes the result. Mafic, iron-rich rocks yield iron oxides, granitic iron-poor rocks yield aluminum ores, and ultramafic rocks yield nickel laterites. The process slowed with abrupt global cooling and continues today at a reduced rate.

soil-form-083.title: Stonelayers: buried stones that trace the land surface
soil-form-083.text: A stonelayer is a subsurface soil layer dominated by particles coarser than 2 mm, and it generally mimics the shape of the ground above. One stone thick, it shows in a pit as a stone line; several stones thick, it is a stone zone. Its stones may be quartz-rich rock fragments, iron–manganese nodules, artifacts, shells or precious stones. It often acts as a subsurface drain or even holds groundwater. Stone lines in soils follow the surface and their stones do not overlap like shingles, pointing to a soil origin. Water-laid stone lines in sediments do overlap, and their origin is geological.

soil-form-059.title: Biorhexistasy: climate swings between building and stripping soil
soil-form-059.text: In 1951 the pedologist Henry Erhart proposed that climate switches the land between two phases, biostasy and rhexistasy. In biostasy, abundant regular rain under protective vegetation drives chemical alteration, eluviation and illuviation. Eluvial horizons, clay-enriched horizons and sesquioxide-rich subsoils build up. In rhexistasy, a drier climate thins the vegetation and soil formation slows. Physical weathering dominates, and intense rains erode soils into layers of sand and silt. Pleistocene glacial periods are considered times of rhexistasy, and interglacials times of biostasy.

soil-form-064.title: Pedodiversity: counting soils the way ecologists count species
soil-form-064.text: In 1995 Ibáñez and colleagues counted soils the way ecologists count living things. They first applied ecological diversity indices, richness, relative abundance and the Shannon index, treating soil classes as taxa. Pedodiversity is the variation of soil properties within an area, usually expressed through soil classes. Studies began with how the number of soil classes grows with area, in work by Beckett and Bie in 1978. McBratney developed the term in 1992 while discussing landscape preservation. A 2003 US study found the West richest in soil taxa. At the finest level, taxa increased steadily with area, a sign of considerable soil endemism. Variety can be very local. In eastern North Carolina and the Ouachita Mountains, variability within plots, tied to individual trees and local rock, outweighed differences between plots. Conventional indices ignore how similar soil classes are. The mean soil taxonomic distance, which accounts for it, has been shown to be a better measure. Knowing natural pedodiversity helps preserve the soil cover and rebuild quasi-natural soils on degraded land.
